title: Don't buy smart glasses, Dutch data watchdog advises
description: The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wro
body: The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.It said in its tests of six glasses available on the Dutch market, the devices advised a user on how to date a child, misread medicine instructions, and claimed to have called an ambulance when they had not.While the AP is advising people not to buy the smart glasses, it stopped short of calling for them to be banned from sale.The authority is not revealing which glasses it tested, saying only that prices ranged from under €100 (£84) to over €500 and originated from different continents.The research follows growing concerns about privacy risks associated with smart glasses, in particular the misuse of the tech to film women without consent, or to record in places where filming is usually prohibited such as healthcare settings.Meta, a leading seller of the glasses, recently released a version without a camera with some commentators suggesting this was a response to the privacy backlash.It is unknown if the investigation included Meta's glasses. The AP told the BBC it would not name the products it tested.The BBC has approached Meta, TCL and HTC - all major manufacturers of smart glasses - for comment. Previously, these firms have been keen to highlight positive uses of smart glasses.Meta has highlighted the assistance they can provide to people with visual impairments. Its smart glasses use AI to describe things in the wearer's environment or to read text.The AP recognises the glasses can be valuable for people who need help to understand their surroundings. But for these users, it argues it is particularly important that AI is reliable.AP said in its testing of the unnamed brands, it found the advice given could be wrong.During a simulated emergency in which CPR resuscitation advice was requested, the AP found one pair of glasses claimed several times an ambulance was on the way - but emergency services had not been contacted.It said the AI also made child protection errors, with potentially serious consequences.One pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who indicated a romantic interest in a minor.The glasses also made errors when reading instructions inside medicine packages, as well as with interpreting severe weather warnings.And the AP was concerned smart glasses could be used to secretly film people, highlighting the ease with which lights, which warn that a device is recording, could be obscured.It said with some glasses these lights could be covered with tape and they would still work, despite some manufacturers claiming they would not function.Meanwhile, in some glasses, the AP found serious security flaws which meant someone nearby could connect without permission, view recordings, or even operate the camera remotely.It warned data recorded by the glasses was often exported outside the EU.In February, reports revealed outsourced workers were able to view sensitive content recorded on Meta smart glasses Meta said at the time such workers might sometimes review content, including video and images, in order to help improve its AI.It said it took the protection of people's data very seriously, and was constantly refining its efforts and tools in that area, and would filter it first to blur faces in images.The AP investigation was not primarily focused on data protection - instead it was concerned with algorithms and AI.In the UK Paul Arnold, chief executive of privacy watchdog the Information Commission, who has a severe visual impairment has previously stressed the complexity of the argument, external around smart glasses."They can help me and others better understand our surroundings, access information and navigate the world with greater confidence," he wrote in September.But he said he had been "shocked and appalled by some of the irresponsible and harmful ways people are using these technologies".

schema.headline: Don't buy smart glasses, Dutch data watchdog advises

title: The Brexit debate is back - and there are nerves about what happens next
description: "Stop Me If You Think You've Heard This One Before" sang Morrissey, as part of The Smiths in 1987, shortly before the band's acrimonious divorce.It's
body: "Stop Me If You Think You've Heard This One Before" sang Morrissey, as part of The Smiths in 1987, shortly before the band's acrimonious divorce.It's a lyric Brexit veterans might be humming to themselves this week. Maybe even the prime minister, who is an avid fan of the Manchester band.Some of the names - and arguments - that defined the Brexit period inside and outside Parliament are starting to emerge again, as the debate about the UK's relationship with the EU returns."It's like déjà vu with knobs on," said one veteran of the Leave campaign to us.A new group called Stay Out has been set up, backed by figures who were part of the official Leave campaign in 2016. Boris Johnson has been back in the headlines, saying he still thinks Britons would choose to be outside the bloc.Pro-EU groups such as the European Movement are raising their voices, pointing to the range of politicians, diplomats and academics they have supporting their argument. And a steady stream of Labour figures are now emerging to say they want to rejoin.The former Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy made the argument on the BBC on Wednesday, saying Labour should go into the next election backing renegotiating membership of the EU and then putting that to people in another referendum.He joins a list of cabinet ministers under Sir Keir Starmer who want to revisit EU membership; a list that includes former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, former Business Secretary Peter Kyle and former Welsh Secretary Jo Stevens. Others who served around Sir Keir's cabinet table think the same privately.That is significant. Yes, they all backed Remain in 2016. But these are figures who were part of a government elected on a manifesto saying it was important to make Brexit work. They set red lines in that manifesto because they thought the public had moved on. But they have now decided to say - most of them very publicly - that they think the picture has changed and the UK needs to think again.The prime minister has opened the door to all options, from single market membership to rejoining the customs union to a referendum on full membership.But in recent days, his language has softened a little from the clear commitment in his party conference speech that around the time of this Friday's summit he would "lay out to the country" the different options for Britain's long-term relationship with Brussels.After some confusion about when this would take place, the government now says this will happen around the time that Burnham presents his 10-year plan, right before Parliament's Christmas break.Burnham's allies say this will allow him to tie his EU policy more closely to his domestic agenda, arguing that a different arrangement with Europe would help with his other priorities such as the cost of living and re-industrialisation. Others worry that the all-consuming nature of the EU debate means that it will drown out the other parts of the 10-year plan.What remains unclear is the timeframe for the process that will follow Burnham setting out what he sees as the different Brexit options. The prime minister has always been clear that Labour's commitments in its 2024 manifesto not to rejoin the single market or the customs union - let alone the EU altogether - still stand until the next general election. And it was to those manifesto red lines that Burnham returned when asked about rejoining the EU at PMQs on Wednesday.Yet those would not preclude Burnham initiating negotiations now on an arrangement breaking those red lines, which would take effect after the next general election.Nevertheless, some on the prime minister's own side ponder that - having turned the volume up on the whole issue this autumn - he might be wise to turn it down a little in the new year, so it doesn't risk drowning out other things ministers want to talk about.Andy Burnham is a prime minister who likes to explore things out loud. It's part of what he sees as a new way of doing politics, where he answers questions honestly and is prepared to discuss ideas while they are being formed, not just after they are a settled position. It is a style that seeks to present a sense of a desired direction, even if some of the specifics end up being walked back from.But even though it might be some time before the government has an official position on the future relationship, plenty of people are discussing what might happen next."It is all go again! My inbox is full of the same old stuff I thought I'd seen the back of years ago," one senior figure told us.There are some nerves in the Labour Party about what might happen next. MPs who we have spoken to hold a range of views, which shows why this won't be plain-sailing.Some are worried about re-opening the debate, calling it "toxic".Others worry that the prime minister could disappoint pro-EU voters if he doesn't go far enough.Others still wonder if the argument has changed enough that voters would decide differently in a new referendum."Both sides need fresh arguments, not the ones we all got tired of last time," said one."If this just looks like politicians wanting to rejoin because they never got over leaving then it's dead on arrival. "If we can show that actually this is being led by businesses, by farmers, by different parts of society who need to rejoin because of the ways Brexit has harmed them, then it's a different matter," said another.And what would the new EU the UK could rejoin look like? Some Labour MPs ponder that the EU is changing – with the possibility of more right-wing leaders at the top table. They question whether they would want to be part of that.A long standing diplomat from an EU member state said that the possibility of political change within the EU, alongside the recent offer of associate membership to Canada and at least the possibility of a potential future arrangement with Ukraine after any peace deal, could mean Brussels becomes more open to looser forms of membership that it has not been willing to consider before.But then there is Scotland. If the government backs another EU vote, some Scottish MPs worry it adds to the argument for another vote on Scottish independence.Despite the warnings, plenty of MPs are delighted that the Europe debate is back on the agenda.One summed it up like this: "It doesn't really matter to me at this point where the PM is heading on this – it's all good for appealing to progressive voters. Just being seen to talk about this even without it necessarily being clear what we're going to do is a big change from before."That seems to be a prevailing mood at the moment. Lots of Labour MPs are happy the EU debate is back. But not all of them.Andy Burnham will on Friday sign a new deal with the EU which ministers believe will drive economic growth and cut red tape for British businesses. It will be heralded as a new moment for the relationship.But how much further could the reset go?The government hasn't decided yet - but plenty of others have their own views.

schema.headline: The Brexit debate is back - and there are nerves about what happens next

title: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByHelen BushbyCulture reporterFlorence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByHelen BushbyCulture reporterFlorence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent appearance at the Governors Awards, and denied speculation about weight-loss drugs and facial surgery. The actress wrote on Instagram, external how "stressful" it was waking up to people "talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend". "I have never been on Ozempic. I have never done any face surgery," she wrote. "And don't ever say that I didn't make my own nose, I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!"She added: "For the first time in my entire career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily."In her eight-page statement, the Oppenheimer, Dune and East of Eden star told followers: "I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pugh has spoken out before about judgement about how women look Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds"."The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg."Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming". "I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again"."I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."Professor Heather Widdows from Everyday Lookism, external, which campaigns to end body shaming, told BBC News: "Pugh is right that we are in a place where 'beauty standards are changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with'. "A global beauty ideal makes impossible demands and normalises what were once extreme," added Widdows, who is Professor of Philosophy at the University of Warwick. "We know that body-shaming individuals is harmful. Given this, we should not say negative things about other people's bodies... in a world where our bodies are increasingly ourselves, when you shame bodies you shame people."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pugh is no stranger to a striking red carpet outfit Pugh, who was Oscar-nominated for Little Women in 2020 and played Black Widow assassin Yelena Belova in this year's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has previously spoken out against judgement about women's looks.In 2024, she told the Times, external she aimed to "challenge how women were perceived"."Look, not everybody has legs that go on for days. I remember watching this industry and feeling that I wasn't represented," she said. "I've loved challenging ideas I don't like."She also spoke about why she thinks she receives criticism about her appearance. "I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that," she said. "But now this...? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives."Pugh did not have comments turned on for her post, but it was liked by celebrities including Ashley James, who is known for speaking out about body positivity, plus Carol Vorderman, Zoe Ball, writer and actress Katy Brand and doctor and broadcaster Amir Khan.  'Please be gentle'Pugh also said she had sued several publications earlier this year, claiming they published AI-generated images appearing to show her receiving cosmetic injections that were presented as real photographs."I was... horrified," she wrote, claiming the articles had damaged her reputation.The actress concluded by urging followers to think about their attitudes towards physical appearance."I understand that we are in a warped part of image history right now, with beauty standards changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with," she said. "But please be gentle to yourselves and others when you go in on people's physical appearance."I'm not angry at you, I'm angry at the situation that's being projected onto us."It feels inescapable, but part of changing the tide is on you as much as us in the public eye."

schema.headline: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation

title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
description: European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv."Europe has
body: European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv."Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing. Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks"."That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable". Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition. Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions. Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine"."These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen."A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine. It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory. As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not."I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

schema.headline: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

title: EU-UK talks going down to the wire, says No 10
description: Negotiations between the EU and UK are "going down to the wire" ahead of Friday's summit in Brussels, Downing Street has said. The summit is aimed at
body: Negotiations between the EU and UK are "going down to the wire" ahead of Friday's summit in Brussels, Downing Street has said. The summit is aimed at reaching new agreements between the two sides on food trade rules, visas for young people and carbon emissions pricing. Sources have told the BBC the UK is set to agree to a quota of 100,000 young people per year coming to the UK as part of a new youth mobility scheme. Downing Street has not commented on the details, which would also allow young Britons to live in Europe.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions and debates" of the Brexit referendum. Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, she said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but added "not trade at any cost". She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc. Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from the deal on Friday."There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said."But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow."So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal is secured, the government will introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes. A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK. The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India. In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement. Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in the talks, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students. An agreement on trade could also remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling. On immigration, Burnham has said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.The prime minister has said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU. However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun, external, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU. He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

schema.headline: EU-UK talks going down to the wire, says No 10

title: England: Football Association punished by Uefa after fans' anti-Catholic chants against Spain in Nations League
description: England have been punished by Uefa following anti-Catholic chanting from the away fans during their Nations League victory in Spain.European football'
body: England have been punished by Uefa following anti-Catholic chanting from the away fans during their Nations League victory in Spain.European football's governing body have fined the Football Association £12,572 (15,000 euros) and imposed a suspended one-match ban for England away supporters.BBC Sport understands the charge of 'racist and/or discriminatory behaviour' relates to chants that were deemed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish.A further offence within the next two years would mean a ban on away fans is enforced.There had been concerns of the prospect of racist chanting from Spain fans before the game in Madrid with England boss Thomas Tuchel stating he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture.Tuchel stressed he didn't expect any incidents, but the visit was England's first to the Spanish capital since a notorious 2004 encounter at the Bernabeu was overshadowed by racist chanting directed at their players.That led to a firm response from Spain head coach Luis de la Fuente, who said: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism."Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."England won the match 3-2 to end Spain's 43-match unbeaten run and top League A Group 3.

schema.headline: England: Football Association punished by Uefa after fans' anti-Catholic chants against Spain in Nations League

title: Sir James Cleverly named as Tory candidate in mayor of London 2028 race
description: Labour incumbent Lord Khan, first elected in 2016, is yet to confirm whether he will seek a fourth term.Sir James, a former head of the London Fire Au
body: Labour incumbent Lord Khan, first elected in 2016, is yet to confirm whether he will seek a fourth term.Sir James, a former head of the London Fire Authority, was widely expected to win the nomination after he stood down from the shadow cabinet in August. He said he would not seek re-selection as the candidate in his Essex seat at the next general election.At the announcement of the result, he said Lord Khan was "letting London down".Sir James added: "People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place - businesses, job creators, families leaving London - and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related."The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause. When I ask Londoners, 'Do you feel safe walking home at night?', the answer is no.""It's shameful, it's a failure, and it's not just crime."We have had the worst period of housebuilding since the Second World War and only the highest-earning Londoners can afford the cheapest houses in London."Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, said: "James Cleverly has a record of failure and now wants to inflict his disastrous CV on London."He backed a no-deal Brexit and Liz Truss's disastrous mini-budget, voted for cuts to policing and youth services and opposed action to clean up London's air."Londoners should never forgive and never forget the damage the Conservatives did to our capital."Sir James, an Army reservist, represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015.After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative Party leader in 2024, losing out to Kemi Badenoch.The only other confirmed party choice for the mayoral race is Laila Cunningham from Reform UK, whose candidacy was announced in January.She told BBC London: "It's the Conservatives that cut police, they cut the magistrates' numbers, crime went up, they politicised stop and search, and as a result knife crime has gone up massively."Sarah Olney and Rob Blackie are both candidates for the Liberal Democrats' nomination.Olney, the MP for Richmond Park, told BBC London the city "really needs a champion but the Tories are not going to be able to effectively hold Labour to account given their record in the capital".She added: "James Cleverley simply is not a credible contender for mayor of London. "In the past decade he has enthusiastically championed Brexit and he was a huge supporter of Liz Truss's mini budget and both of those things have done so much damage to London."Should Lord Khan decide not to run again, there are a number of London Labour figures with ambitions to be the next mayor, including MPs Dawn Butler and Rosena Allin-Khan.The Green Party, which won outright control of three London boroughs at the local elections in May, leads minority administrations in Haringey and Lambeth, and runs Southwark in coalition with the Lib Dems, has yet to begin the process of picking a candidate for the 2028 mayoral race.Mayor of Hackney Zoë Garbett, who was the Green candidate in the 2024 mayoral election, said Sir James would "take London backwards".She added: "Cleverly's platform is all about dividing our communities and making people's lives harder and more expensive."Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

schema.headline: Sir James Cleverly named as Tory candidate in mayor of London 2028 race

title: Ella Langley sweeps Country Music Awards as Taylor Swift performs with Keith Urban
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Ella Langley said her hit Choosin' Texas was "the gift that keeps on giving"BySteven McIntoshEntertainment reporte
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Ella Langley said her hit Choosin' Texas was "the gift that keeps on giving"BySteven McIntoshEntertainment reporter US singer Ella Langley has swept the Country Music Association Awards (CMAs), following the huge success of her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas.The Alabama-born singer was named entertainer of the year at Wednesday's ceremony, weeks after the song became the longest-running number one in Billboard chart history."At this point, I'm sick of me," the 27-year-old joked in her acceptance speech, having spent so much of the ceremony on stage. "I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life."Choosin' Texas was also named single of the year and song of the year, leading Langley to joke in an acceptance speech: "This song is the gift that keeps on giving." Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ella Langley, who won six awards on the night, performed her song Loving Life AgainLangley won six awards in total, including female vocalist of the year, music video of the year and album of the year for Dandelion.She also performed her song Loving Life Again with a string quartet, and duetted with Miranda Lambert for a performance of Snakeskin Boots.Choosin' Texas made history in September after spending 23 weeks at the top spot on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. It has now spent 28 weeks in total at the summit.Following her win, Langley took to social media and said: "Hard to put this night into words and what it means."Thank you to my fans. Thank you for loving this record, thank you for coming to my shows, thank you for believing in my artistry."This year has been the most incredible journey, and I want to thank you for sharing in that with me. I love y'all."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Langley also performed Snakeskin Boots with Miranda Lambert during the ceremonyTaylor Swift also performed at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years.Her performance began with Swift walking backstage and featured cameo appearances from country stars including Brad Paisley, Little Big Town, Sugarland, and Brooks & Dunn.Swift then sang her recent hit I Knew It, I Knew You, from the Toy Story 5 soundtrack, using a blue guitar with bedazzled clouds on it, in a nod to the animated franchise.The singer also mixed in some of her 2006 country hit Our Song, while Keith Urban joined her on the banjo.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Taylor Swift used a Toy Story-themed guitar and performed alongside Keith UrbanImage source, ReutersImage caption, She also presented a lifetime achievement award to country music duo Brooks & DunnSwift's performance came after she was inducted into both the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame earlier this year. Other winners on the night included Chris Stapleton who won male vocalist of the year, The Red Clay Strays who won vocal group of the year, and Brooks & Dunn with vocal duo of the year.Meanwhile Stephen Wilson Jr won the new artist of the year award while Charlie Worsham won musician of the year.The award ceremony began with a tribute to country music legend Dolly Parton, who died in August aged 80.Ceremony host Lainey Wilson began the tribute by duetting with singer-songwriter Vince Gill on a rendition of Parton's I Will Always Love You.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The night opened with a tribute to country legend Dolly Parton, who died aged 80 in AugustImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Vince Gill and Lainey Wilson performed I Will Always Love You in tribute to PartonImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Presenters at the ceremony included actor Glen Powell and ShaboozeyImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Kix Brooks and Ronnie Dunn, known as Brooks & Dunn, accepted the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement AwardImage source, ReutersImage caption, There was also a firey performance of Who Told You That during the ceremony from Tucker WetmoreImage source, ReutersImage caption, Megan Moroney delivered a floral performance of Beautiful ThingsImage source, ReutersImage caption, Other winners included Chris Stapleton, who took home male vocalist of the yearImage source, Getty Images

title: Mykhailo Mudryk: Andriy Shevchenko disputes player's doping claims
description: Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federatio
body: Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federation to "falsely" take the blame for the winger's positive drugs test.Tottenham winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.The 25-year-old said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk firmly placed the blame for his 20-month absence from the sport on his national association, which has led to Shevchenko's response.In a statement, former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko, who is now president of the UAF, said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally" and called on the player to retract his words.He added: "His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample. "The UAF refused, as such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work."He added that "numerous investigations and audits" undertaken as part of the case were unable to shed light on when or where the substance entered Mudryk's system.In his interview Mudryk also claimed Shevchenko had offered him little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and said its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.However, Shevchenko went on to say that national team staff had complied with a request from Chelsea not to provide Mudryk with any medication while on international duty. And he also challenged the former Shakhtar Donetsk forward to provide evidence "to back up his words"."Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps," Shevchenko added."These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine."The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case."I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism. "If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question."BBC Sport has contacted Mudryk's representatives for comment.

schema.headline: Mykhailo Mudryk: Andriy Shevchenko disputes player's doping claims

title: Trump China summit with Putin and Xi high on spectacle
description: So far, however, the US has been remarkably silent following the three-party meeting. While China was quick to release a joint communique detailing th
body: So far, however, the US has been remarkably silent following the three-party meeting. While China was quick to release a joint communique detailing the discussions and Putin expounded during an hour-long post-meeting press conference, Trump has made minimal public comments, instead promising a news conference at the White House on Friday.On his trip to China earlier this year and following his meeting with Xi at the APEC summit in South Korea last October, Trump spoke with the press early in his flight back to Washington.For the moment, the White House is letting the joint communique, released Thursday after the three met, do the talking. But the document is mostly a vague endorsement of efforts to ensure "strategic stability and international security".That, along with the visuals of three powerful men sitting in the same room to amicably discuss global issues, might offer some reassurance no catastrophic conflicts are on the horizon. But pledges of further "dialogue" and an acknowledgement that nuclear war "must never be fought" provide minimal substance beyond the rhetoric."In general, it's good for the leaders of the major global players to come together in various formats, even if the results appear to be modest at best," David Firestein, head of the Bush Foundation for US-China Relations, told the BBC.A line about boosting "the production and supply of refined petroleum products" seems directed at Putin, given that nation's role as a major source of fossil fuels on the international market. And it was hard to miss the condemnation of the International Criminal Court – a recent target of American ire.If there's one thing the leaders of the three major world powers can agree on, it's that multilateral global organisations that attempt to enforce international law shouldn't have the teeth to back up those efforts.While in China, Trump called Putin his "friend", and praised his "outstanding personal relationship" with Xi after sharing a handshake and hug with the Chinese leader.  But once Trump returns to Washington, he is likely face a political environment where views of his Asia trip range from measured concern to outright criticism."I am concerned by how we are characterising our relationships with geopolitical adversaries. Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends," Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah said in a statement to the BBC on Thursday. "Diplomacy is important, but it should never come at the expense of clarity about who our adversaries are."Democrats, for their part, did not mince words."American security cannot be traded away for photo opportunities or personal aggrandisement," nine senators on the foreign relations committee wrote in a letter to the White House.Trump is hardly the first American president to seek an international diplomatic breakthrough as a salve following domestic political setbacks. Democrats Bill Clinton and Barack Obama took overseas trips as presidents shortly after their party's own midterm electoral defeats.In those cases, any boosts to their standing proved short-lived. And while Trump may have gotten the images he wanted from his Asian summit, the lack of substantive progress accompanying them likely means this trip also will be quickly forgotten.Brandon Drenon contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Trump China summit with Putin and Xi high on spectacle

title: Jeremy Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
description: The people who framed the Convention in the years after World War Two, led by Raphael Lemkin, a Jewish survivor of the Holocaust, deliberately set a h
body: The people who framed the Convention in the years after World War Two, led by Raphael Lemkin, a Jewish survivor of the Holocaust, deliberately set a high bar of proof.That is why it has taken so long for the ICJ to deliver a ruling that genocide has been committed.In an ideal world for lawyers and investigators, they would assemble evidence from government documents and military orders. In practice, that is hard if not impossible to get.Governments harbouring genocidal intent do not publicise their objectives. Instead, the Court has inferred evidence of genocidal intent from the actions taken by Myanmar's security forces and local militias against the Rohingya people.According to Janina Dill, Chair in Global Security at the Blavatnik School of Government of the University of Oxford, "Genocidal intent can be inferred from a pattern of conduct… It does not mean the commission of atrocities had to follow only one goal, genocide. If that were the case, demonstrating that atrocities also followed other goals (like counterinsurgency, punishment or displacement) would negate genocidal intent."The court was incredibly clear that these are plausible goals, but it ruled that the totality of the evidence cannot be explained without genocide being one objective."In other words, even if a state has been attacked, and if it orders its forces on to the offensive claiming self-defence, the sum of its actions could add up to genocide.The justices made clear that each case needed to be treated on its merits. But because the court's decisions affect the way the law is interpreted, the Myanmar case does have an impact on the other genocide cases that are being heard by the ICJ. The most prominent is the one brought by South Africa against Israel over the killing and destruction it has inflicted on Palestinians in Gaza.The British barrister, Philippe Sands KC, part of the Gambia's legal team, was in the chamber of the ICJ in The Hague to hear the verdict. Sands told the BBC's World at One programme that when they were arguing the case against Myanmar at the ICJ in January this year, Gaza was "the elephant in the room. Everybody knew that the court's approach in this case would have implications in the next one".The approach taken by the ICJ justices in the judgement on Myanmar, he told the BBC, clarifies the standard of evidence they require to prove genocide."If the Gambia had lost, South Africa's case would, in effect, be over."But the Gambia now having succeeded, the door remains open for South Africa. That doesn't mean that South Africa will win. It doesn't mean that the International Court of Justice will find there was a genocide in Gaza. It means that the evidentiary standard has been defined very clearly, and it will be now for the parties in that next case and in other cases to meet those standards."The undoubted joy and relief felt by Rohingyas in the camps in Bangladesh will not deliver them an immediate improvement in the miserable and dangerous living conditions they have been forced to endure for almost a decade.The court has no mechanism to enforce its rulings, but it has told Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingyas.That will not be easy. Hundreds of villages have been razed to the ground, and the Myanmar government is unlikely quietly to accept the verdict of the court.The UK, as the so-called "pen holder" on the UN Security Council with responsibility for diplomacy around the Myanmar issue, put out a statement saying it was "determined to act and ensure accountability for these appalling crimes… we must ensure the Court's ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity".It has called for an urgent session of the Security Council, is expelling Myanmar's defence attaché in London and has promised other measures in the coming days.  Not much might be possible at the UN. A tough resolution against Myanmar could be vetoed by either China or Russia, or both.Other rumblings have come from the Trump Administration about the case. Without waiting for the ICJ's verdict, former US President Joe Biden's administration declared in 2022 that the Myanmar military committed genocide against the Rohingya people.But Mike Waltz, the current US ambassador to the UN, warned the court last month not to "lower the legal threshold for proving genocide".Waltz said he was speaking out to protect "American and allied soldiers" but his post has been widely interpreted as support for Israel's defence at the ICJ.He condemned what he called the "leftist, global, antisemitic agenda" of the international community, singling out Navi Pillay, this year's recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, who was one of the judges in the Myanmar case.She led a UN independent international commission that reported a year ago that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.

schema.headline: Jeremy Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications

title: Mauricio Pochettino: New manager's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator
description: Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by
body: Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances."For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it," said the drone operator."The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage."The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the managers first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."The session was also filmed by United's own media channel, who regularly film club training sessions.Civil Aviation Authority guidelines include the following warning: "If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you're likely to be breaking data protection laws."Manchester United have declined to comment.There were 10 outfield players working with Pochettino, although it seems unlikely it will be the starting line-up for Sunday's trip to Liverpool.While Harry Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo are regular starters, Ayden Heaven and Andrey Santos have had less involvement, and neither Joshua Zirkzee nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Jaume Camacho 17, who is yet to feature at senior level, was also with the group.On an adjoining pitch, skipper Bruno Fernandes is shown in one group playing the 'rondos' game, where two players are in the middle trying to intercept the passes of the five players in a circle on the outside. Youngster Shea Lacey and last season's FA Youth Cup-winning skipper Dan Armer are also involved, along with England youth international Bendito Mantato. Next to that is another group which includes more experienced players in Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount, Leny Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot. The identical twins Jack and Tyler Fletcher are split between the two groups, with Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez across both.Not all the players were identifiable and United confirmed defender Patrick Dorgu was involved.

schema.headline: Mauricio Pochettino: New manager's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator

title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in first-of-its kind IPO
description: Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the public stock market, taking its valu
body: Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the public stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion.The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 per share, showing there is plenty of excitement around AI.Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.5, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day, with shares hitting $97.Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet (down 3%) and Amazon (down 3.9%).The build-out happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble."Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate more quickly tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet.It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market."There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth $1.5 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available."We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.On Thursday, the same day Anthropic went public, a bipartisan group of lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product"."AI carries real risks," she added.Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

schema.headline: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in first-of-its kind IPO

title: Faults not fixed in 90% of homes in government insulation scheme
description: More than 90% of homes fitted with faulty insulation under energy-saving government schemes have not yet had repairs completed to fix the botched work
body: More than 90% of homes fitted with faulty insulation under energy-saving government schemes have not yet had repairs completed to fix the botched work, a minister has said.The government found almost all homes that had external wall insulation installed as part of two of the government's ECO schemes had defects that needed repairing.Speaking to a committee of MPs on Wednesday, Energy Minister Martin McClusky said repair works had been completed at 2,227 out of the 24,600 homes impacted.He said he was shocked by the extent of the failures and has assured affected households they would not be asked to pay to sort out these problems.McClusky told MPs the insulation schemes "didn't have correct oversight".Ofgem oversees the ECO schemes and alongside TrustMark, a government-backed consumer protection service, is responsible for auditing homes to identify faulty installations.The government and its partners have known about significant levels of defective and unsafe insulation for years, with audits finding poor work in October 2024.Ken Palfrey, a 66-year-old retired builder from Birmingham, is among the home owners waiting for repairs.He had external wall insulation installed through the ECO programme in 2024.He claims the installation was "botched", causing damage to his window sills and leading to damp and mould on his walls.He said he complained and after some months an inspection concluded the insulation had been fitted incorrectly and he was told it had to be removed immediately.Palfrey said for two years he had been on a "merry-go-round", spending "hundreds and hundreds of hours writing emails and complaining to people".Earlier this month, TrustMark referred his case to the National Energy Foundation (NEF), a charity that has funding from energy suppliers to put right damaged homes where the installer has gone out of business."It's been an absolute nightmare," Palfrey said."Every day of my life, every time you look at the insulation, you're worried about it."A TrustMark spokesperson said it was working to contact affected households and to fix "the unacceptable problems left by this faulty external wall insulation scheme". "We're sorry for what Mr Palfrey has been through and have referred him to the National Energy Foundation which should be able to get his insulation put right," the spokesperson said.Labour MP Bill Esterson, the chair of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, told the BBC he was seeking assurances that the victims "will be supported in a timely fashion".But he said he was concerned that Ofgem, Great Britain's energy regulator, had "failed to identify whether work had been carried out or completed to a decent standard".When asked if he had confidence in Ofgem at the committee, McClusky did not answer the question directly.He said: "There's clearly been failures in the system. We're designing a system now."He added Ofgem was a "very different organisation than it was a number of years ago".A spokesperson for Ofgem said: "It is unacceptable that households have been left with substandard ECO4 work. Ofgem was not responsible for assuring the quality of installations."The spokesperson said the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) "is responsible for the design and overall outcomes of ECO, and that Ofgem's role did not include assessing installation quality"."Our role, set by government, is to administer the scheme and hold suppliers to account for meeting their obligations," the Ofgem spokesperson added. "When serious quality problems emerged, we went beyond our core role to support affected households and help establish the scale of the problem."The BBC has asked TrustMark for comment.The two ECO schemes that have caused widespread issues are known as ECO4 and Great British Insulation Scheme (GBIS).ECO4 was launched in 2022 and since then, more than 300,000 homes have had heat pumps, solar panels and insulation fitted under the £4bn scheme. It is closing in December.GBIS - which opened in 2023 and has now closed - was more narrowly designed to help households lower their energy bills by installing cheap insulation.The BBC has been reporting on the impact of faulty insulation installed under these schemes in recent years.Fuel Poverty Action, a campaign group, argues that problems with faulty upgrades under a range of government energy efficiency schemes could be affecting as many as 100,000 homes."Ignoring the other defective measures is shockingly negligent, and is causing huge harm," said Jonathan Bean, policy lead at Fuel Poverty Action."Defective internal wall insulation causes major hidden damage, making it a ticking time bomb in homes."The government estimates that 29% of it is defective but chose not to include it in the Find and Fix process."A spokesperson for DESNZ said: "We inherited the failing ECO4 scheme, which we ended after it clearly let families down."No household should have to pay to put the issues right and TrustMark is working to support those affected to ensure this is the case."Our Warm Homes Plan will overhaul the system to protect consumers and ensure failings are not repeated."

schema.headline: Faults not fixed in 90% of homes in government insulation scheme
